definitions.explanation: A canid native to East Asia with a distinctive masked face. Not related to raccoons despite the English name. Tanuki are significant in Japanese folklore as shapeshifters.

examples.japanese: {狸|たぬき}が{道|みち}を{横切|よこぎ}って{行|い}った。
{信楽焼|しがらきやき}の{狸|たぬき}の{置物|おきもの}は{有名|ゆうめい}だ。
{日本|にほん}の{昔話|むかしばなし}には{狸|たぬき}が{人|ひと}を{化|ば}かす{話|はなし}が{多|おお}い。
examples.english: In Japanese folktales, there are many stories of tanuki tricking people.

notes:
{狸|たぬき} refers to the Japanese raccoon dog, a species unique to East Asia.

Common expressions:
- {狸|たぬき}そば (soba with tenkasu/tempura crumbs)
- {狸寝入|たぬきねい}り (pretending to be asleep)
- {狸|たぬき}{親父|おやじ} (sly old man)
- {狐|きつね}と{狸|たぬき}の{化|ば}かし{合|あ}い (battle of wits between sly people)
- {取|と}らぬ{狸|たぬき}の{皮算用|かわざんよう} (don't count your chickens before they hatch)

Counter: {匹|ひき}

Cultural note:
The ceramic {狸|たぬき} statues with large bellies, straw hats, and sake bottles seen outside restaurants are from {信楽|しがらき} in Shiga Prefecture. In folklore, tanuki can shapeshift and are often depicted as playful tricksters, in contrast to the more cunning {狐|きつね}.
